claim: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a major cause of human death.
source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a major cause of human death.
evidence: This is a general statement about CRC mortality that draws from established medical knowledge.

claim: CRC mortality is primarily due to metastatic organ colonization, with the liver being the main organ affected.
source: Mortality is primarily due to metastatic organ colonization, with the liver being the main organ affected.
evidence: This statement reflects established clinical knowledge about CRC metastasis patterns.

claim: PDX modeling of CRC predicted patient survival outcomes.
source: Such PDX modeling predicted patient survival outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing correlation between PDX characteristics and patient survival.

claim: In vivo selection of multiple PDXs for enhanced metastatic colonization capacity upregulated the gluconeogenic enzyme PCK1.
source: In vivo selection of multiple PDXs for enhanced metastatic colonization capacity upregulated the gluconeogenic enzyme PCK1, which enhanced liver metastatic growth by driving pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthesis under hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic profiling data and qRT-PCR measurements showing PCK1 upregulation in liver metastatic derivatives.

claim: PCK1 enhanced liver metastatic growth by driving pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthesis under hypoxia.
source: In vivo selection of multiple PDXs for enhanced metastatic colonization capacity upregulated the gluconeogenic enzyme PCK1, which enhanced liver metastatic growth by driving pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthesis under hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by metabolite profiling, isotope tracing experiments, and functional assays showing PCK1's role in pyrimidine biosynthesis and hypoxic growth.

claim: Highly metastatic tumors upregulated multiple pyrimidine biosynthesis intermediary metabolites.
source: Consistently, highly metastatic tumors upregulated multiple pyrimidine biosynthesis intermediary metabolites.
evidence: This is supported by metabolite profiling data showing increased levels of orotate, dihydroorotate, and ureidopropionate in metastatic PDXs.

claim: Therapeutic inhibition of DHODH with leflunomide substantially impaired CRC liver metastatic colonization.
source: Therapeutic inhibition of the pyrimidine biosynthetic enzyme DHODH with leflunomide substantially impaired CRC liver metastatic colonization and hypoxic growth.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experiments showing reduced liver colonization and improved survival in leflunomide-treated mice.

claim: Leflunomide substantially impaired CRC hypoxic growth.
source: Therapeutic inhibition of the pyrimidine biosynthetic enzyme DHODH with leflunomide substantially impaired CRC liver metastatic colonization and hypoxic growth.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro hypoxia cell viability assays showing reduced growth under hypoxic conditions.

claim: An estimated 145,000 Americans will be diagnosed with CRC in 2019.
source: An estimated 145,000 Americans will be diagnosed with CRC and roughly 51,000 will die of it in 2019 (National Cancer Institute, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the National Cancer Institute.

claim: Roughly 51,000 Americans will die of CRC in 2019.
source: An estimated 145,000 Americans will be diagnosed with CRC and roughly 51,000 will die of it in 2019 (National Cancer Institute, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the National Cancer Institute.

claim: The majority of CRC deaths are due to distant metastatic disease with the liver being the most common distal organ colonized.
source: The majority of these deaths are due to distant metastatic disease with the liver being the most common distal organ colonized (National Cancer Institute, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the National Cancer Institute and represents established clinical knowledge.

claim: A significant fraction of patients diagnosed with non-metastatic or locoregional CRC will experience subsequent metastatic progression.
source: While the prognosis of patients diagnosed with non-metastatic or locoregional disease is relatively better, a significant fraction of such patients will nonetheless experience subsequent metastatic progression.
evidence: This reflects established clinical knowledge about CRC progression patterns.

claim: Few prognostic indicators of CRC metastatic disease progression exist.
source: A key clinical need is identifying which patients will develop metastatic disease since few prognostic indicators of disease progression exist.
evidence: This reflects the current state of clinical knowledge and unmet medical needs.

claim: Tissue culture drift, adaptation, and evolution can restrict the relationship of cell lines to the pathophysiology of patient tumors.
source: While cell lines established from human CRC have provided important insights into the biology of CRC, tissue culture drift, adaptation, and evolution can restrict their relationship to the pathophysiology of patient tumors (Gillet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Gillet et al., 2013.

claim: PDX models can capture the endogenous diversity within a tumor as well as the patient-to-patient variability of metastatic cancer.
source: Patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models, which allow for the growth of patient tumor samples in immunodeficient mice, can capture the endogenous diversity within a tumor as well as the patient-to-patient variability of metastatic cancer.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the advantages of PDX models.

claim: Breast cancer, melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer PDX modeling can predict human clinical outcomes.
source: Prior work has revealed that breast cancer, melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer PDX modeling can predict human clinical outcomes (Quintana et al., 2012; John et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Past CRC PDX models were subcutaneous implantations.
source: Past CRC PDX models were subcutaneous implantations (Cho et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Subcutaneous PDX tumors do not metastasize.
source: Such subcutaneous PDX tumors are useful for tumor growth studies, but do not metastasize and are not exposed to the pathophysiologically relevant and restrictive conditions of the hepatic microenvironment.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the limitations of subcutaneous xenograft models.

claim: Subcutaneous PDX tumors are not exposed to the pathophysiologically relevant and restrictive conditions of the hepatic microenvironment.
source: Such subcutaneous PDX tumors are useful for tumor growth studies, but do not metastasize and are not exposed to the pathophysiologically relevant and restrictive conditions of the hepatic microenvironment.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the differences between subcutaneous and hepatic microenvironments.

claim: Orthotopic PDX implantation has limited feasibility in CRC because the orthotopic tumor kills the host due to obstructive dimensions prior to liver metastatic colonization.
source: While orthotopic PDX implantation serves as a good model for studying metastasis in melanoma and breast cancer, this approach has limited feasibility in CRC, as the orthotopic tumor kills the host due to the obstructive dimensions that implanted tumors reach prior to liver metastatic colonization (Quintana et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on cited work and practical observations about CRC orthotopic models.

claim: 48.3% of subjects' CRC samples engrafted subcutaneously.
source: Thirty-one subjects provided 40 tumor samples; 48.3% of the subjects' samples engrafted (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly measured data from the PDX experiments.

claim: The majority of subjects in this study were classified as Stage IV CRC according to the AJCC.
source: The majority of subjects in this study were classified as Stage IV CRC according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC).
evidence: This is descriptive data about the patient cohort.

claim: AJCC stage was not associated with increased xenograft engraftment (p=0.35).
source: However, AJCC stage was not associated with increased xenograft engraftment (p=0.35; χ2 test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The engraftment rates for tumor tissues that originated from the colon and the liver were similar (40% vs 37.5%).
source: The engraftment rates for tumor tissues that originated from the colon and the liver were similar (40% vs 37.5%; Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly measured data from the PDX experiments.

claim: 67.7% of subjects had undergone chemotherapy prior to surgical resection of metastases.
source: Most subjects had undergone chemotherapy prior to surgical resection of metastases (67.7%).
evidence: This is descriptive data about the patient cohort.

claim: MSI-H tumors exhibited the highest engraftment rates (83.3%).
source: When categorizing tumors by commonly tested clinical mutations (KRAS, high microsatellite instability (MSI-H), NRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, and none), MSI-H tumors exhibited the highest engraftment rates (83.3%), while tumors lacking these commonly tested for clinical mutations exhibited the lowest engraftment rates (18.2%).
evidence: This is directly measured data from the PDX experiments.

claim: Tumors lacking commonly tested clinical mutations exhibited the lowest engraftment rates (18.2%).
source: When categorizing tumors by commonly tested clinical mutations (KRAS, high microsatellite instability (MSI-H), NRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, and none), MSI-H tumors exhibited the highest engraftment rates (83.3%), while tumors lacking these commonly tested for clinical mutations exhibited the lowest engraftment rates (18.2%).
evidence: This is directly measured data from the PDX experiments.

claim: Subcutaneous tumor engraftment was associated with worse patient survival (p=0.045).
source: We found that subcutaneous tumor engraftment was associated with worse patient survival (p=0.045; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The time from subcutaneous tumor implantation to tumor harvest ranged from 35 to 88 days.
source: The time from subcutaneous tumor implantation to tumor harvest ranged from 35 to 88 days (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly measured data from the PDX experiments.

claim: Among CRC tumors that grew subcutaneously, the time required to reach 1000 mm3 was not significantly associated with patient survival (p=0.27).
source: Among those CRC tumors that did grow subcutaneously, the time required to reach the pre-determined tumor size (1000 mm3) was not significantly associated with patient survival (p=0.27; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of survival data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Successful liver metastatic colonization was achieved upon injection of 15/17 patient samples.
source: Successful liver metastatic colonization was achieved upon injection of 15/17 patient samples.
evidence: This is directly measured data from the PDX experiments.

claim: The time to mouse sacrifice for the CRC patient-derived liver xenografts ranged from 51 to 407 days.
source: The time to mouse sacrifice for the CRC patient-derived liver xenografts ranged from 51 to 407 days (Figure 2D) and did not correlate with subcutaneous tumor growth rates (R2 = 0.046, p=0.50; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly measured data from the PDX experiments.

claim: Liver colonization time did not correlate with subcutaneous tumor growth rates (R2 = 0.046, p=0.50).
source: The time to mouse sacrifice for the CRC patient-derived liver xenografts ranged from 51 to 407 days (Figure 2D) and did not correlate with subcutaneous tumor growth rates (R2 = 0.046, p=0.50; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The mCRC liver PDXs fell into two biologically distinct groups based on their growth rates: one set grew quickly (within three months), the other set grew more slowly (after 6 months or 1 year).
source: The mCRC liver PDXs fell into two biologically distinct groups based on their growth rates: one set grew quickly, requiring mouse euthanasia within three months of implantation; the other set grew more slowly, requiring animal sacrifice after 6 months, or even 1-year, post-engraftment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The two groups of PDXs with different liver growth rates exhibited similar growth rates when implanted subcutaneously (p=0.09).
source: Importantly, these two groups of PDXs exhibited similar growth rates when implanted subcutaneously (p=0.09; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Distinct selective pressures exist in the liver relative to the subcutaneous microenvironment.
source: This suggests distinct selective pressures existing in the liver relative to the subcutaneous microenvironment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that liver and subcutaneous growth rates are not correlated.

claim: Patients whose xenografts rapidly colonized mouse livers fared poorly relative to patients whose xenografts colonized the liver slowly or not at all (p=0.031).
source: We found that the liver colonization model mimicked clinical outcomes, as patients whose xenografts rapidly colonized mouse livers fared poorly relative to patients whose xenografts colonized the liver slowly or not at all (p=0.031; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of survival data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CRC liver metastasis PDX modeling is prognostic of clinical survival outcome.
source: Taken together, these results establish that CRC liver metastasis PDX modeling described above is prognostic of clinical survival outcome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the survival correlation data.

claim: Both subcutaneous and liver engrafted tumors re-capitulated the architecture of the primary tumor from which they were derived.
source: Contrary to this, we observed that both subcutaneous and liver engrafted tumors re-capitulated the architecture of the primary tumor from which they were derived (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CLR4 remained poorly differentiated in both the subcutaneous and liver xenografts.
source: CLR4 was established from a poorly differentiated liver metastatic colon adenocarcinoma; it remained poorly differentiated in both the subcutaneous and liver xenografts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CLR32 and CLR28 retained moderate-to-well differentiated histology when passaged subcutaneously and hepatically.
source: Similarly, CLR32 and CLR28 were derived from moderate-to-well differentiated primary colon and peritoneal metastatic adenocarcinomas and retained moderate-to-well differentiated histology when passaged subcutaneously and hepatically (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In each of the four CRC PDX comparisons, the in vivo-selected CRC PDX liver metastatic derivatives colonized the mouse liver more efficiently than their parental counterparts.
source: In each of the four CRC PDX comparisons, the in vivo-selected CRC PDX liver metastatic derivatives colonized the mouse liver more efficiently than their parental counterparts (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly measured data from the in vivo selection experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The hypoxia signature was the most significantly enriched gene signature in liver metastatic derivatives (NES = 2.12, q-value <0.001).
source: The hypoxia signature was found to be upregulated in all the liver metastatic derivatives individually and in the composite, where it was the most significantly enriched gene signature (normalized enrichment score (NES) = 2.12, q-value <0.001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of transcriptomic data.

claim: Upregulation of hypoxia genes in the liver metastatic derivatives is consistent with hypoxia being an important feature of the liver metastatic microenvironment.
source: Upregulation of hypoxia genes in the liver metastatic derivatives is consistent with previous reports demonstrating that hypoxia is an important feature of the liver metastatic microenvironment (Loo et al., 2015; Nguyen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by cited prior work.

claim: 24 genes were significantly upregulated across the four pairs of CRC PDXs with an effect size of greater than 1.5 log2 fold change.
source: Using this approach, we identified 24 highly upregulated genes in the liver metastatic derivatives (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), with the 10 most highly upregulated genes annotated on the volcano plot (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis using Fisher's combined probability test.

claim: Two of the top ten upregulated genes (IFITM1 and CKB) have been previously implicated as promoters of CRC metastasis.
source: Interestingly, two of the top ten upregulated genes (IFITM1, and CKB) have been previously implicated as promoters of CRC metastasis (Loo et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Three of the candidate genes were enzymes (ACSL6, CKB and PCK1) and one was a cell-surface receptor (CDHR1).
source: In the list of candidate genes, three were enzymes (ACSL6, CKB and PCK1) and one was a cell-surface receptor (CDHR1).
evidence: This is a classification of the identified genes based on their known functions.

claim: The 24-gene CRC liver colonization signature was significantly enriched (p=0.007) in liver metastases from patients with CRC.
source: The upregulated genes were significantly enriched (p=0.007) in the bin with the most upregulated genes in CRC liver metastases (Figure 4B) (Goodarzi et al., 2009), supporting the clinical relevance of our in vivo-selected CRC PDX liver colonization mouse model.
evidence: This is based on analysis of a publicly available patient dataset (Sheffer et al., 2009).

claim: The gene expression upregulation in the metastatic CRC PDX system significantly correlated (rho = 0.39, p=0.047) with the gene expression upregulation in human liver CRC metastases relative to CRC primary tumors.
source: In further support of the clinical relevance of our findings, we found that the gene expression upregulation in our metastatic CRC system significantly correlated (rho = 0.39, p=0.047) with the gene expression upregulation in human liver CRC metastases relative to CRC primary tumors (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis between PDX and patient data.

claim: PCK1 was highly upregulated in human CRC liver metastases relative to primary tumors.
source: Interestingly, PCK1 was highly upregulated in human CRC liver metastases relative to primary tumors.
evidence: This is based on analysis of publicly available patient datasets.

claim: QPCR quantification confirmed PCK1 up-regulation in liver metastatic derivatives relative to isogenic parental counterparts.
source: QPCR quantification confirmed PCK1 up-regulation in liver metastatic derivatives relative to isogenic parental counterparts (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PCK1 was significantly upregulated (p=0.01) in CRC liver metastases relative to primary tumors in the GSE50760 dataset.
source: We analyzed other publicly available CRC gene expression datasets and consistently observed PCK1 to be significantly upregulated (p=0.01, Student's t-test; Figure 4E) in CRC liver metastases relative to primary tumors (Figure 4E–G) (Kim et al., 2014; Stange et al., 2010; Ki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on analysis of a publicly available patient dataset.

claim: PCK1 was upregulated (p=0.01) in CRC liver metastases in the GSE14297 dataset containing paired CRC primary tumors and CRC liver metastases from the same patients.
source: Additionally, PCK1 was upregulated (p=0.01; Figure 3F, p<0.0001; Figure 4G) in CRC liver metastases in datasets containing only paired CRC primary tumors and CRC liver metastases obtained from the same patients (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of a publicly available paired patient dataset.

claim: PCK1 was upregulated (p<0.0001) in CRC liver metastases in the GSE6988 dataset containing paired CRC primary tumors and CRC liver metastases from the same patients.
source: Additionally, PCK1 was upregulated (p=0.01; Figure 3F, p<0.0001; Figure 4G) in CRC liver metastases in datasets containing only paired CRC primary tumors and CRC liver metastases obtained from the same patients (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of a publicly available paired patient dataset.

claim: Depletion of PCK1 in SW480 cells by two independent shRNAs significantly impaired (p<0.0001 in both comparisons) CRC liver metastatic colonization.
source: Depletion of PCK1 in SW480 cells by two independent shRNAs significantly impaired (p<0.0001 in both comparison) CRC liver metastatic colonization of cells introduced into the portal circulation of NSG mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on in vivo liver colonization experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PCK1 depletion in LS174T cells significantly decreased (p<0.0001) liver metastatic colonization.
source: PCK1 depletion in another colorectal cell line (LS174T) also significantly decreased (p<0.0001) liver metastatic colonization (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on in vivo liver colonization experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PCK1 over-expression in SW480 cells significantly increased (p=0.003) liver metastatic colonization.
source: Conversely, PCK1 over-expression in SW480 cells significantly increased (p=0.003) liver metastatic colonization (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on in vivo liver colonization experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PCK1 depletion did not impact subcutaneous tumor growth in the SW480 or LS174T cell lines.
source: In contrast, PCK1 depletion did not impact subcutaneous tumor growth in the SW480 or LS174T cell lines (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on subcutaneous tumor growth experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Pck1 depletion decreased murine CRC cell liver colonization in an immune competent model (p=0.039, p=0.005 for shCTRL vs shPck1-64, shCTRL vs shPck1-66, respectively).
source: Consistent with our observations in human cancer lines, Pck1 depletion decreased murine CRC cell liver colonization in an immune competent model (p=0.039, p=0.005 for shCTRL vs shPck1-64, shCTRL vs shPck1-66, respectively) and did not impair in vitro proliferation under basal cell culture conditions (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on in vivo liver colonization experiments in immunocompetent mice shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Pck1 depletion in CT26 cells did not impair in vitro proliferation under basal cell culture conditions.
source: Consistent with our observations in human cancer lines, Pck1 depletion decreased murine CRC cell liver colonization in an immune competent model (p=0.039, p=0.005 for shCTRL vs shPck1-64, shCTRL vs shPck1-66, respectively) and did not impair in vitro proliferation under basal cell culture conditions (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on in vitro cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PCK1 depletion after initial liver colonization (days 0-4) continued to impair (p=0.004) CRC metastatic liver growth.
source: We found that even after the initial liver colonization phase (days 0–4), PCK1 depletion continued to impair (p=0.004) CRC metastatic liver growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is based on inducible PCK1 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: PCK1 depletion did not increase apoptosis in both PCK1 depleted cell populations in vivo.
source: We did not observe increased apoptosis using the caspase 3/7 reporter in both PCK1 depleted cell populations in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on in vivo apoptosis measurements using caspase 3/7 reporter shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PCK1 modulation altered the rate of in vivo growth in each experiment where a luciferase reporter was used.
source: Evaluation of the in vivo growth rate through natural log slope calculations demonstrated that in each PCK1 modulation experiment, either knockdown or overexpression, in which a luciferase reporter was used, the rate of growth after the first measured time point (day 4–7) did not equal the rate of growth of the controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on growth rate analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PCK1 promotes the rate of metastatic growth in vivo.
source: These results reveal that PCK1 promotes the rate of metastatic growth in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the growth rate analysis data.

claim: PCK1 depletion significantly reduced CRC cell growth under hypoxia.
source: Consistent with this, PCK1 depletion significantly reduced CRC cell growth under hypoxia, an effect not observed under normoxia (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on hypoxia cell viability assays shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PCK1 depletion did not reduce CRC cell growth under normoxia.
source: Consistent with this, PCK1 depletion significantly reduced CRC cell growth under hypoxia, an effect not observed under normoxia (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on normoxia cell viability assays shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hypoxia poses a metabolic challenge for cancer cell growth as metabolites needed for biosynthesis of macromolecules required for cell proliferation can become limiting.
source: Hypoxia poses a metabolic challenge for cancer cell growth as metabolites needed for biosynthesis of macromolecules required for cell proliferation can become limiting (Birsoy et al., 2015; Garcia-Bermudez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Three out of four PDX pairs showed increased abundance of multiple nucleoside base precursors and specifically metabolites in the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway.
source: Interestingly, the most salient observation was increased abundance in three out of four PDX pairs of multiple nucleoside base precursors and specifically metabolites in the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Metastatic colonization by human CRC cells selects for induction of multiple metabolites in the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway.
source: These findings reveal that metastatic colonization by human CRC cells selects for induction of multiple metabolites in the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metabolite profiling data.

claim: PCK1 was previously shown to promote ribose generation by CRC cells under pathophysiological levels of glucose via the pentose phosphate pathway.
source: PCK1 was previously shown to promote ribose generation by CRC cells under pathophysiological levels of glucose via the pentose phosphate pathway (Montal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: PCK1 depleted cells showed significant depletion of nucleosides and nucleotides including uridine, guanine, UMP, CMP, CDP, IMP, GMP, and AMP under hypoxia.
source: While metabolites related to glycolysis and the citric acid (TCA) cycle were significantly increased, corroborating previous studies (Montal et al., 2015), the most salient finding was a significant depletion of nucleosides and nucleotides including uridine, guanine, UMP, CMP, CDP, IMP, GMP, and AMP in PCK1 depleted cells (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is based on metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: The observed decreases in nucleoside and nucleotide levels in PCK1-depleted cells were abrogated under normoxic conditions.
source: Consistent with our observations of selective impairment of PCK1-dependent growth under hypoxia, the observed decreases in nucleoside and nucleotide levels were abrogated under normoxic conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is based on metabolite profiling data under normoxia shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Increased PCK1 expression is required for nucleotide pool maintenance in CRC cells in the context of hypoxia.
source: These findings reveal that increased PCK1 expression is required for nucleotide pool maintenance in CRC cells in the context of hypoxia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metabolite profiling data under hypoxia and normoxia.

claim: The generation of pyrimidine precursors (aspartate and orotate) by reductive carboxylation was significantly decreased upon PCK1 depletion.
source: Glutamine labeling revealed that the generation of pyrimidine precursors, such as aspartate and orotate, by reductive carboxylation was significantly decreased upon PCK1 depletion (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: This is based on 13C glutamine metabolic flux analysis shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: The generation of pyrimidine precursors derived from oxidative reactions in the TCA cycle were either significantly increased or unchanged upon PCK1 depletion.
source: In contrast, the generation of pyrimidine precursors derived from oxidative reactions in the TCA cycle were either significantly increased or unchanged (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is based on 13C glutamine metabolic flux analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: PCK1 promotes reductive carboxylation under hypoxia to produce pyrimidine precursor aspartate.
source: These findings reveal that PCK1 promotes reductive carboxylation under hypoxia to produce pyrimidine precursor aspartate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 13C glutamine metabolic flux analysis.

claim: Aspartate has been shown to be sufficient to enable growth under hypoxia or electron transport chain dysfunction.
source: Aspartate has been shown to be sufficient to enable growth under hypoxia or electron transport chain dysfunction (Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Supplementation of PCK1-depleted cells with aspartate partially rescued the observed hypoxic growth defect.
source: Supplementation of PCK1-depleted cells with aspartate partially rescued the observed growth defect, while pyruvate supplementation provided a modest rescue (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Pyruvate supplementation provided a modest rescue of the hypoxic growth defect in PCK1-depleted cells.
source: Supplementation of PCK1-depleted cells with aspartate partially rescued the observed growth defect, while pyruvate supplementation provided a modest rescue (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Combined aspartate and pyruvate supplementation nearly fully rescued the hypoxic growth defect of PCK1-depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, combined aspartate and pyruvate supplementation nearly fully rescued the hypoxic growth defect of PCK1-depleted cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: PCK1 promotes growth by maintaining the levels of aspartate, a nucleotide precursor.
source: These findings reveal that PCK1 promotes growth by maintaining the levels of aspartate, a nucleotide precursor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with aspartate.

claim: PCK1 may additionally promote hypoxic growth by increasing NAD+ pools.
source: The increased hypoxic growth observed upon combined aspartate and pyruvate supplementation suggest the possibility that PCK1 may additionally promote hypoxic growth by increasing NAD+ pools.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: Supplementation of CRC cells with uridine rescued the hypoxic growth defect caused by PCK1 depletion.
source: Indeed, supplementation of CRC cells with uridine rescued the hypoxic growth defect caused by PCK1 depletion.
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments with uridine.

claim: Supplementation with purines or ribose provided a modest effect on rescuing the hypoxic growth defect caused by PCK1 depletion.
source: In contrast, supplementation with purines or ribose provided a modest effect (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments shown in Figure 6I.

claim: PCK1 induction is a mechanism employed by CRC cells to generate pyrimidine nucleotide pools under hypoxia to fuel growth.
source: These findings reveal PCK1 induction to be a mechanism employed by CRC cells to generate pyrimidine nucleotide pools under hypoxia to fuel growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments and metabolite profiling data.

claim: Pre-treatment of cells with 3 MPA significantly reduced (p=0.01) mCRC liver colonization in vivo.
source: Similar to PCK1 inhibition by shRNA, pre-treatment of cells with 3 MPA significantly reduced (p=0.01) mCRC liver colonization in vivo (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A),
evidence: This is based on in vivo liver colonization experiments with 3 MPA pre-treatment shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Pre-treatment of LS174T cells with 3 MPA did not alter subcutaneous tumor growth.
source: Pre-treatment of LS174T cells with 3 MPA did not, however, alter subcutaneous tumor growth (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on subcutaneous tumor growth experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Short-term treatment of 3 MPA decreased CRC liver colonization (p=0.008; p=0.005).
source: We found that even such short-term treatment of 3 MPA decreased CRC liver colonization in this model (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) (p=0.008; p=0.005 for Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C respectively).
evidence: This is based on in vivo liver colonization experiments with oral gavage of 3 MPA shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PCK1 promotes colorectal cancer liver colonization and represents a potential therapeutic target in the prevention of CRC at risk for metastatic disease.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that PCK1 promotes colorectal cancer liver colonization and represents a potential therapeutic target in the prevention of CRC at risk for metastatic disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional and pharmacological inhibition experiments.

claim: Leflunomide treatment significantly impaired CRC growth in the context of hypoxia.
source: Leflunomide treatment significantly impaired CRC growth in the context of hypoxia—an effect that was more significant under hypoxia than normoxia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays under hypoxia and normoxia shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Metastatic CRC cell growth under hypoxia is sensitive to pyrimidine biosynthesis inhibition.
source: These findings confirm that metastatic CRC cell growth under hypoxia is sensitive to pyrimidine biosynthesis inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the leflunomide treatment experiments.

claim: DHODH depletion substantially reduced CRC liver metastatic colonization.
source: DHODH depletion substantially reduced CRC liver metastatic colonization (Figure 7D), revealing a critical role for DHODH activity and pyrimidine biosynthesis in CRC liver metastatic colonization.
evidence: This is based on in vivo liver colonization experiments with DHODH knockdown shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Treatment of animals with leflunomide caused a ~90 fold reduction in CRC liver metastatic colonization.
source: Treatment of animals injected with highly metastatic Lvm3b cells with leflunomide caused a ~ 90 fold reduction in CRC liver metastatic colonization (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on in vivo liver colonization experiments with leflunomide treatment shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Leflunomide treated mice experienced significantly longer survival (p=0.006) than the control mice.
source: The leflunomide treated mice experienced significantly longer survival (p=0.006) than the control mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Lvm3b cells are known to be highly resistant to 5-FU.
source: Importantly, these cells are known to be highly resistant to 5-FU (Bracht et al., 2010), the backbone chemotherapeutic used in CRC, revealing that inhibition of DHODH can exert therapeutic benefit despite cellular resistance to an anti-metabolite that targets the pyrimidine pathway.
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Inhibition of DHODH can exert therapeutic benefit despite cellular resistance to 5-FU.
source: Importantly, these cells are known to be highly resistant to 5-FU (Bracht et al., 2010), the backbone chemotherapeutic used in CRC, revealing that inhibition of DHODH can exert therapeutic benefit despite cellular resistance to an anti-metabolite that targets the pyrimidine pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the leflunomide efficacy in 5-FU resistant cells.

claim: Leflunomide treatment only modestly impacted primary tumor growth by two distinct CRC populations.
source: Leflunomide treatment only modestly impacted primary tumor growth by two distinct CRC populations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–H), suggesting enhanced sensitivity of CRC cells to leflunomide-mediated DHODH inhibition during liver metastatic colonization.
evidence: This is based on primary tumor growth experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: CRC cells exhibit enhanced sensitivity to leflunomide-mediated DHODH inhibition during liver metastatic colonization.
source: Leflunomide treatment only modestly impacted primary tumor growth by two distinct CRC populations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–H), suggesting enhanced sensitivity of CRC cells to leflunomide-mediated DHODH inhibition during liver metastatic colonization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of leflunomide on primary tumor growth versus liver metastatic colonization.

claim: The impaired growth upon hypoxia caused by leflunomide was rescued upon uridine supplementation.
source: To determine if the metastatic colonization defect caused by leflunomide treatment is caused by pyrimidine depletion, we tested cell growth suppression in the presence or absence of uridine—the downstream metabolic product of the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway. This revealed that the impaired growth upon hypoxia was rescued upon uridine supplementation (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments with uridine shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Leflunomide treatment impaired proliferation significantly more in the context of hypoxia than under normoxia.
source: Importantly, leflunomide treatment impaired proliferation significantly more in the context of hypoxia than under normoxia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is based on cell viability assays under hypoxia and normoxia shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Highly metastatic cells exhibit enhanced dependence on pyrimidine biosynthesis.
source: These observations reveal enhanced dependence of highly metastatic cells on pyrimidine biosynthesis and reveal upregulation of metabolites in this pathway as a selective adaptive trait of highly metastatic CRC cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the leflunomide sensitivity experiments and metabolite profiling data.

claim: Upregulation of metabolites in the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway is a selective adaptive trait of highly metastatic CRC cells.
source: These observations reveal enhanced dependence of highly metastatic cells on pyrimidine biosynthesis and reveal upregulation of metabolites in this pathway as a selective adaptive trait of highly metastatic CRC cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metabolite profiling data showing increased pyrimidine metabolites in metastatic derivatives.

claim: DHODH is a therapeutic target in CRC progression.
source: Overall, these findings identify DHODH as a therapeutic target in CRC progression and provide proof-of-concept for use of leflunomide in therapeutic inhibition of CRC metastatic progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DHODH inhibition experiments.

claim: Leflunomide can be used for therapeutic inhibition of CRC metastatic progression.
source: Overall, these findings identify DHODH as a therapeutic target in CRC progression and provide proof-of-concept for use of leflunomide in therapeutic inhibition of CRC metastatic progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the leflunomide treatment experiments.

claim: Successful subcutaneous tumor engraftment is associated with worse patient survival in CRC.
source: Similar to others, we found that successful subcutaneous tumor engraftment associated with worse patient survival in those with CRC (Oh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis data and cited from prior work.

claim: Among tumors that engrafted subcutaneously, the subcutaneous tumor growth rate did not significantly correlate with patient survival.
source: However, among those tumors in our study that did engraft subcutaneously, the subcutaneous tumor growth rate did not significantly correlate with patient survival.
evidence: This is based on survival analysis data.

claim: Liver metastatic growth rate was significantly correlated with patient survival.
source: In contrast, we found that liver metastatic growth rate was significantly correlated with patient survival.
evidence: This is based on survival analysis data.

claim: The discrepancy in the prognostic power of subcutaneous tumor growth versus liver metastatic growth is likely due to the greater selective pressure inherent to the liver microenvironment.
source: The reason for this discrepancy in the prognostic power of subcutaneous tumor growth versus liver metastatic growth is likely the greater selective pressure inherent to the liver microenvironment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in prognostic power.

claim: Epidemiologic data suggests that patients with diabetes on metformin exhibit improved CRC clinical outcomes relative to their metformin-free counterparts.
source: Epidemiologic data suggests that those patients with diabetes that are on metformin, a gluconeogenic-antagonist, exhibit improved CRC clinical outcomes relative to their metformin-free counterparts (Zhang et al., 2011; Spillane et al., 2013; Fransgaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior epidemiologic studies.

claim: The findings provide a potential mechanistic basis for the sensitivity of CRC metastatic progression to inhibition of the gluconeogenic pathway.
source: Our observations suggest a potential mechanistic basis for the sensitivity of CRC metastatic progression to inhibition of this metabolic pathway.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to epidemiologic observations about metformin.

claim: PCK1 was found to enhance melanoma tumor re-initiation.
source: In one study, PCK1 was found to enhance melanoma tumor re-initiation (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Melanoma 'tumor re-initiating cells' consumed more glucose and produced more lactate and glycerate-3-phosphate.
source: In this work, the authors demonstrated that, in tissue culture, melanoma 'tumor re-initiating cells' consumed more glucose and produced more lactate and glycerate-3-phosphate; PCK1 silencing elicited the opposite phenotype in culture (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Montal et al. described a mechanism by which PCK1 promotes CRC growth through its increased ability to metabolize glutamine into lipids and ribose.
source: Using cell culture metabolomics, Montal et al. (2015) recently described a mechanism by which PCK1 promotes CRC growth through its increased ability to metabolize glutamine into lipids and ribose .
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: PCK1 silencing in a CRC cell line in vitro decreased glutamine utilization and TCA cycle flux.
source: PCK1 silencing in a CRC cell line in vitro was shown to decrease glutamine utilization and TCA cycle flux (Montal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Cells with increased expression of PCK1 consumed more glucose and produced more lactate.
source: This group found that cells with increased expression of PCK1 consumed more glucose and produced more lactate.
evidence: This is cited from prior published work (Montal et al., 2015).

claim: PCK1 staining on a primary CRC tissue microarray showed that PCK1 was overexpressed in many primary CRC biopsies but its expression was not associated with tumor grade.
source: They further performed PCK1 staining on a primary CRC tissue microarray, finding that PCK1 was overexpressed in many primary CRC biopsies but its expression was not associated with tumor grade.
evidence: This is cited from prior published work (Montal et al., 2015).

claim: Three recent studies demonstrated that PCK2 upregulation in lung cancer cells in vitro can improve cancer cell survival in glucose-depleted conditions.
source: While we did not find evidence of PCK2 upregulation in our mCRC model, three recent studies demonstrated that PCK2 upregulation in lung cancer cells in vitro can improve cancer cell survival in glucose-depleted conditions (Leithner et al., 2015; Vincent et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: In glucose-depleted conditions, lung cancer cells increased consumption of glutamine as an energy source in a PCK2-dependent manner.
source: Vincent et al. found that in glucose-depleted conditions, lung cancer cells increased consumption of glutamine as an energy source in a PCK2-dependent manner.
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Zhao et al. observed PCK2 upregulation in tumor initiating cells and demonstrated that PCK2 promoted tumor initiation through reducing TCA cycle flux by lowering Acetyl-CoA.
source: Zhao et al. (2017) observed PCK2 upregulation in tumor initiating cells and demonstrated that PCK2 promoted tumor initiation through reducing TCA cycle flux by lowering Acetyl-CoA.
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Increased PCK1 strongly drives liver metastatic colonization but minimally impacted primary tumor growth rate in the cells studied.
source: First, we demonstrate that increased PCK1 strongly drives liver metastatic colonization but minimally impacted primary tumor growth rate in the cells studied.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing differential effects on liver versus subcutaneous growth.

claim: PCK1 can promote hypoxic growth.
source: Second, we provide the first reported evidence that PCK1 can promote hypoxic growth.
evidence: This is based on the hypoxia cell viability assays.

claim: PCK1 plays a key role in pyrimidine biosynthesis under hypoxia via reductive carboxylation.
source: Third, we uncover a key role for PCK1 in pyrimidine biosynthesis under hypoxia via reductive carboxylation.
evidence: This is based on the metabolite profiling and isotope tracing experiments.

claim: Zamboni et al. reported that in a bacterium with pyruvate kinase impairment, PCK1 could operate in reverse—converting phosphoenolpyruvate to oxaloacetate.
source: Although we do not provide a precise biochemical mechanism by which PCK1 promotes reductive carboxylation, Zamboni et al. (2004) reported that in a bacterium with pyruvate kinase impairment, PCK1 could operate in reverse—converting phosphoenolpyruvate to oxaloacetate.
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Metabolite profiling of PCK1-depleted cells under hypoxia revealed increased abundance of phosphoenolpyruvate.
source: In support of this, our metabolite profiling of PCK1-depleted cells under hypoxia revealed increased abundance of phosphoenolpyruvate.
evidence: This is based on metabolite profiling data.

claim: Highly metastatic CRC cells upregulate PKLR, which was shown to inhibit pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) activity.
source: Moreover, we had previously observed that highly metastatic CRC cells upregulate PKLR, which was shown to inhibit pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) activity (Nguyen et al., 2016)—analogous to the observations in the aforementioned bacterial study.
evidence: This is cited from prior published work by the authors.

claim: Recent work has implicated DHODH as a regulator of differentiation in myeloid leukemia.
source: Recent work has implicated DHODH as a regulator of differentiation in myeloid leukemia as well as a promoter of cell cycle progression in some solid cancer types such as melanoma and pancreatic adenocarcinoma (White et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: DHODH is a promoter of cell cycle progression in some solid cancer types such as melanoma and pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
source: Recent work has implicated DHODH as a regulator of differentiation in myeloid leukemia as well as a promoter of cell cycle progression in some solid cancer types such as melanoma and pancreatic adenocarcinoma (White et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Bajzikova et al. found that de-novo pyrimidine biosynthesis is essential for mouse breast cancer tumorigenesis in a DHODH-dependent manner.
source: Bajzikova et al. found that de-novo pyrimidine biosynthesis is essential for mouse breast cancer tumorigenesis in a DHODH-dependent manner (Bajzikova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: CRC metastatic progression selects for upregulation of pyrimidine biosynthesis.
source: Our work reveals that beyond effects on cell growth in vitro and primary tumor growth, CRC metastatic progression selects for upregulation of pyrimidine biosynthesis.
evidence: This is based on the metabolite profiling data showing increased pyrimidine metabolites in metastatic derivatives.

claim: The use of leflunomide to therapeutically target DHODH has been implicated under various cancer contexts as a metabolic inhibitor.
source: Moreover, the use of leflunomide to therapeutically target DHODH has been implicated under various cancer contexts as a metabolic inhibitor (Mathur et al., 2017; Luengo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: Hypoxia enhances the sensitivity of cells to DHODH inhibition.
source: Our work reveals that hypoxia enhances the sensitivity of cells to DHODH inhibition, consistent with enhanced pyrimidine biosynthesis enabling enhanced growth under hypoxia—a key feature of the hepatic tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This is based on the differential effects of leflunomide under hypoxia versus normoxia.

claim: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) was the first chemotherapeutic to demonstrate efficacy in reducing the risk of CRC recurrence.
source: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) was the first chemotherapeutic to demonstrate efficacy in reducing the risk of CRC recurrence (Moertel et al., 1990).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work and represents established clinical knowledge.

claim: 5-FU remains the backbone of the current FOLFOX regimen, which is administered to patients after surgical resection to reduce the risk of metastatic relapse.
source: This agent remains the backbone of the current FOLFOX regimen, which is administered to patients after surgical resection to reduce the risk of metastatic relapse.
evidence: This represents established clinical knowledge about CRC treatment.

claim: 5-FU targets thymidylate synthase, an enzyme downstream of DHODH in the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway.
source: Interestingly, 5-FU targets thymidylate synthase, an enzyme downstream of DHODH in the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway—supporting our premise of dependence and susceptibility to inhibition of this pathway in CRC metastasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of action of 5-FU.

claim: A large fraction of patients treated with 5-FU relapse.
source: Despite its activity, a large fraction of patients treated with 5-FU relapse.
evidence: This represents established clinical knowledge about CRC treatment outcomes.

claim: Multiple mechanisms of resistance to 5-FU have been described.
source: Multiple mechanisms of resistance to 5-FU have been described (Holohan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior published work.

claim: PDX modeling of CRC can be predictive of clinical survival outcomes.
source: Overall, our work reveals that PDX modeling of CRC can be predictive of clinical survival outcomes; that integration of PDX modeling with in vivo selection can give rise to highly metastatic PDX derivatives which can be profiled transcriptomically and metabolically to identify key drivers of metastatic progression; and that PCK1 and DHODH represent key metabolic drivers of CRC metastasis and therapeutic targets in CRC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the survival correlation data.

claim: Integration of PDX modeling with in vivo selection can give rise to highly metastatic PDX derivatives which can be profiled transcriptomically and metabolically to identify key drivers of metastatic progression.
source: Overall, our work reveals that PDX modeling of CRC can be predictive of clinical survival outcomes; that integration of PDX modeling with in vivo selection can give rise to highly metastatic PDX derivatives which can be profiled transcriptomically and metabolically to identify key drivers of metastatic progression; and that PCK1 and DHODH represent key metabolic drivers of CRC metastasis and therapeutic targets in CRC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the in vivo selection and profiling experiments.

claim: PCK1 and DHODH represent key metabolic drivers of CRC metastasis and therapeutic targets in CRC.
source: Overall, our work reveals that PDX modeling of CRC can be predictive of clinical survival outcomes; that integration of PDX modeling with in vivo selection can give rise to highly metastatic PDX derivatives which can be profiled transcriptomically and metabolically to identify key drivers of metastatic progression; and that PCK1 and DHODH represent key metabolic drivers of CRC metastasis and therapeutic targets in CRC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the functional and therapeutic inhibition experiments.
